terms.def: NASA's workmanship standard for cables, harnesses and wiring; lacing is §9.2
terms.where: §9.2 Lacing for Trunk, Branches, and Breakouts
terms.quote: 9.2 Lacing for Trunk, Branches, and Breakouts. 9.2.1 When engineering documents specify the use and type of lacing, the following requirements shall apply.

terms.def: The first stitch: a spot tie with a running end
terms.quote: Single-tape starting stitches shall be the same as a spot tie with a running end or as shown in Figure 9-1 View A.

terms.def: A clove hitch followed by a square knot
terms.quote: Spot ties shall consist of a clove hitch followed by a square knot as shown in Figure 9-2 or other non-slip knots.

terms.def: Two crossed turns round the bundle
terms.quote: a clove hitch followed by a square knot as shown in Figure 9-2

terms.def: Ties the clove hitch's two ends off
terms.quote: a clove hitch followed by a square knot

terms.def: The long end that laces on
One tape along the bundle in running lockstitches
terms.quote: Continuous lacing shall be achieved using running lockstitches as shown in Figure 9-5.

terms.def: One turn; the end over, then under: locked
terms.quote: Continuous lacing shall be achieved using running lockstitches as shown in Figure 9-5.

terms.def: Why one cut stitch won't unravel the rest
terms.quote: the "over and under" form is necessary to prevent unraveling of entire cable lacing, in the event one or more stitches are cut

terms.def: Bundle over 25.4 mm (1"): at most 76.2 mm (3") apart
terms.quote: Larger than 25.4 (1.00): 76.2 (3.00) maximum distance between harness ties, mm (in)

terms.def: Where wires leave the main bundle
terms.quote: The separation of a conductor or group of conductors from the main body of wires in a harness.

terms.def: Last lockstitch plus two half hitches
terms.quote: Single or double lacing tape shall be terminated with a closing stitch as shown in Figure 9-3.

terms.def: Round the tape itself, they lock the end

scenes.cue: Lace the cables to the hose
scenes.narration: Loose cables on a LowRider flap, snag and chafe, and can yank a plug mid-cut.

sources.says: "Harness designs and routing shall provide support and protection to harnesses and cables so that they are protected from abrasion, cold flow, cut through, vibration, chafing, flexing, and sharp edges."
"Provision shall be made for stress relief in wires entering connectors from harnesses"

scenes.uncited: "flap" and "snag" are the tutorial's own (the picture shows the loose cables swaying); "yank a plug" is the tutorial's reading of NASA §7.2.28's stress relief at connectors; which cables ride with the core is shown, not said (d19: the problem in one line, the reveal sooner)

more.narration: The fix? Cable lacing: the method NASA specifies for its mission hardware.

sources.says: "This standard applies to production and processing of mission hardware"
"Continuous lacing shall be achieved using running lockstitches as shown in Figure 9-5."
"Cable lacing is a method for tying wiring harnesses and cable looms, traditionally used in telecommunication, naval, and aerospace applications."
"Some organizations have in-house standards to which cable lacing must conform, for example NASA specifies its cable lacing techniques in chapter 9 of NASA-STD-8739.4."

more.narration: Tight, tidy, tough: one tape, no sharp zip-tie tails, and one cut stitch won't unravel the rest.

sources.says: "the \"over and under\" form is necessary to prevent unraveling of entire cable lacing, in the event one or more stitches are cut"

more.uncited: "tight, tidy, tough" and "no sharp zip-tie tails" are the tutorial's own

scenes.cue: Start by the last zip tie
scenes.narration: Following NASA's lacing standard, start beside the core's last zip tie with a spot tie round all three.

sources.says: "Harnesses laced with single tape shall initially be tied with a starting stitch." "Single-tape starting stitches shall be the same as a spot tie with a running end or as shown in Figure 9-1 View A."
"Spot ties shall consist of a clove hitch followed by a square knot as shown in Figure 9-2 or other non-slip knots."
"Some organizations have in-house standards to which cable lacing must conform, for example NASA specifies its cable lacing techniques in chapter 9 of NASA-STD-8739.4."

scenes.narration: Two turns, the second crossing over the first, ends tucked under the cross: a clove hitch grips without slipping.

sources.says: "Spot ties shall consist of a clove hitch followed by a square knot as shown in Figure 9-2 or other non-slip knots."

sources.where: Fig. 9-2 View A (read from the figure)
sources.says: "CLOVE HITCH": two crossed turns round the bundle

scenes.uncited: "Grips without slipping" is the tutorial's wording; NASA §9.2.5 only calls the spot tie's knots non-slip ("or other non-slip knots").

scenes.cue: Right over left, left over right
scenes.narration: Secure it with a square knot: right over left, then left over right, pull snug, and trim the short end.

sources.says: "Spot ties shall consist of a clove hitch followed by a square knot as shown in Figure 9-2 or other non-slip knots."
"CLOVE HITCH AND SQUARE KNOT"
"Lacing tie-ends shall be trimmed."
"Snug the knot tight and trim the short end to about 1/8" or so."

scenes.uncited: "Right over left, then left over right" is the common way to tie a square knot; no surveyed source spells it out.

scenes.narration: Each lockstitch begins with one loose turn of tape round the hose and both cables.

sources.says: "Continuous lacing shall be achieved using running lockstitches as shown in Figure 9-5."
each running lockstitch is one turn round the bundle

scenes.narration: Bring the end back over its standing part, then under the turn; one cut stitch won't unravel the rest.

sources.where: Fig. 9-5; Fig. 9-3's running lockstitch (read from the figure)
sources.says: the end crosses over the standing part, then under the turn's start
"Just remember that the end of the line goes over the standing part and under the round turn so that it binds itself."
"the manner in which the lock stitch is made may vary, but the "over and under" form is necessary to prevent unraveling of entire cable lacing, in the event one or more stitches are cut"

sources.where: Cable lacing, continuous lacing (cites Bureau of Naval Weapons 1962, pp. 7-9 to 7-14, not read)
sources.says: "A series of half-hitches, while visually similar, is not recommended for this application."

scenes.narration: Pull the end along the hose; the loop closes down and grips the bundle.

sources.says: "Continuous lacing shall be achieved using running lockstitches as shown in Figure 9-5."
"The stitch used in keeping the conductors together under pressure is the lock stitch."

scenes.narration: Repeat along the hose: one lockstitch every 68 millimetres (2.7"), each pulled snug before the next.

sources.says: "Continuous lacing shall be achieved using running lockstitches as shown in Figure 9-5."
"Lacing stitches and spot ties shall be placed as detailed in Table 9-1."
harness larger than 25.4 mm (1.00 in): maximum distance between harness ties 76.2 mm (3.00 in)

scenes.narration: Keep the same spacing round the U-turn and back along the lower run, the tape flat on top.

sources.says: "Lacing stitches and spot ties shall be placed as detailed in Table 9-1."
harness larger than 25.4 mm (1.00 in): maximum distance between harness ties 76.2 mm (3.00 in)
"Keeping the lacing tape as flat and free of twists as possible"

scenes.narration: Never leave more than 76 millimetres (3") between stitches, or the cables sag away from the hose.

sources.says: harness larger than 25.4 mm (1.00 in): maximum distance between harness ties 76.2 mm (3.00 in)
"Lacing stitches and spot ties shall be placed as detailed in Table 9-1."

scenes.uncited: "Or the cables sag away from the hose" is the tutorial's reason; NASA states the spacing with no reason.

scenes.narration: Just before the sleeve leaves the hose, the breakout, tie one last lockstitch.

sources.says: "The separation of a conductor or group of conductors from the main body of wires in a harness."
"Lacing shall be terminated at every major breakout or branch" (25 to 30 percent or more of the wire volume); "Closing and starting stitches at branches and breakouts shall be next to the breakout."
"Lockstitching shall terminate with a closing stitch before each large breakout or branch of the harness."
the closing stitch: "LOCKSTITCH PLUS TWO HALF HITCHES"

scenes.cue: Two half hitches lock the end
scenes.narration: Then two half hitches round the tape behind it lock the end, so the lacing can't work loose.

sources.says: "Single or double lacing tape shall be terminated with a closing stitch as shown in Figure 9-3."
the closing stitch: "LOCKSTITCH PLUS TWO HALF HITCHES"
the two half hitches are tied round the tape's own standing part between the running lockstitch and the last lockstitch

scenes.uncited: "So the lacing can't work loose" is the tutorial's reason; NASA gives the closing stitch's form (Fig. 9-3), not its purpose.

scenes.narration: Pull them snug and trim the single tie-off end short.

sources.says: "Lacing tie-ends shall be trimmed."
one tape throughout; its one free end is labelled "TIE-OFF END"
acceptance: "Lacing terminated with a closing stitch and ends trimmed."

scenes.narration: Now watch the core travel: the hose, cord and sleeve flex together, held by every stitch along the run.

more.narration: One last tip: lace with the hose already in its working bend, and keep the tape flat, never twisted.

sources.says: "When bends occur in cable runs, always make the bend before lacing, to keep the bend in place (Figure 9-65)."
"Keeping the lacing tape as flat and free of twists as possible"
"When the conductors are properly laced, they support each other and make a single, neat cable."

scenes.uncited: "Held by every stitch" describes the picture; no source states it.
